result: Adult germ cells in C. elegans rapidly cease mitotic division in response to food removal. In hermaphrodites, M-phase cells dropped from 7.6 to 2.1 within 30 minutes and were virtually absent after 3.5 hours. Males showed similar rapid disappearance of M-phase cells. This response was specific to food removal, as it did not occur in continuously fed or mock-starved controls.
evaluation: Claims C16-C22 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental conditions (hermaphrodites, males, controls) with quantitative measurements and appropriate sample sizes (n=7 replicates of 220-551 gonadal arms). The controls (C19, C20) effectively demonstrate specificity of the response to food removal.

result: Re-feeding of starved animals triggers rapid re-entry into M phase, with hermaphrodites showing a burst of M-phase cells 1.5 hours after re-feeding and males showing a similar response 1 hour earlier. Some individual germlines exhibited approximately twice as many M-phase cells as continuously fed animals, consistent with semi-synchronous M-phase entry.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide direct experimental evidence with appropriate sample sizes. The interpretation of semi-synchronous entry (C28) is a reasonable inference from the observed higher maxima of M-phase cells. The sex difference (C27) is consistent with prior work on cell-cycle timing.

result: Germ cells in L4 hermaphrodites respond differently to starvation than adult germ cells. M-phase cells persist for 4-5 hours after food removal in L4s, with cessation of division coinciding with the molt into adulthood rather than occurring immediately upon food removal.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 provide experimental evidence showing the developmental stage-specific response. The inference that L4 and adult germ cells are not equivalent (C32) is supported by the data and consistent with prior work. The timing correlation with molting was confirmed under different conditions.

result: The timing of M-phase entry upon re-feeding is largely unaffected by the duration of preceding starvation for at least 72 hours.
evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by re-feeding experiments comparing different starvation durations (12, 24, and 72 hours), all showing similar timing of M-phase entry (Figure 2F). This is an important observation distinguishing this system from other quiescence models.

result: Cell-cycle parameters were measured in fed hermaphrodites using EdU labeling. Early adults have a median cell-cycle length of ~6.2 hours (S phase ~4.4 hr, G2 ~1.3 hr, G1+M ~30 min). Hermaphrodites aged 24-hr post mid-L4 have a longer median cell-cycle of ~9.8 hours with a long-tailed G2 distribution.
evaluation: Claims C34-C42 provide detailed cell-cycle measurements using EdU labeling, a standard method. The measurements are consistent with prior work cited in the manuscript. The methodology is described in detail in Materials and Methods, and the long-tailed G2 distribution is consistent with prior observations of variable cell-cycle length.

result: During starvation, germ cells do not pause in G1 but instead progress slowly through S phase and arrest in G2. G1 cells disappear at the same rate as M-phase cells, indicating continued S-phase entry. However, S-phase and G2 fractions change more slowly than expected from fed measurements, indicating slowed S-phase progression.
evaluation: Claims C43-C48 provide a comprehensive analysis of cell-cycle progression during starvation using EdU labeling and nuclear size measurements. The data were collected across multiple age groups and both sexes (n=19-40 gonadal arms per time point). The inference of slow S-phase progression (C48) is well-supported by comparing observed kinetics to fed measurements.

result: Re-feeding restores the rate of progression through S phase and G2. Using emb-30(tn377ts) mutants to trap cells in M phase, 99% of cells entered M phase within 4 hours of re-feeding, faster than the time required to complete S phase and G2 in continuously fed animals.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 use an elegant genetic approach (temperature-sensitive emb-30 mutant) to measure cell-cycle progression upon re-feeding. The quantitative data (55% at 2 hours, 99% at 4 hours) with adequate sample sizes (n=60-66 gonadal arms) support the conclusion that re-feeding restores normal cell-cycle progression rates.

result: Germ cells in germline tumors (glp-1(oz112gf) and gld-3(q730) nos-3(q650)) respond normally to starvation and re-feeding, demonstrating that proximity to the distal tip cell niche is not required for the starvation response. This refines understanding of germ cell fate control, showing that constitutive signaling promotes an undifferentiated fate that still requires food for division.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 provide direct experimental evidence using two different germline tumor genotypes. The inference about germ cell fate control (C56) is well-supported by the observation that even constitutively undifferentiated cells cease division during starvation. Sample sizes are adequate (n=50-249 gonadal arms).

result: Starvation maintains germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch signaling. In fed glp-1(q224ts) animals at restrictive temperature, all germ cells enter meiosis. In starved animals at restrictive temperature, 99% of progenitor zones retain mitotic cells that can re-enter M phase upon re-feeding and maintain long-term self-renewal capacity (91% after 2-3 days recovery).
evaluation: Claims C57-C65 provide compelling evidence using temperature-sensitive glp-1 mutants with appropriate controls. The quantitative data (99% retention, 91% long-term maintenance) with adequate sample sizes (n=148-214 gonadal arms) strongly support the conclusion. Multiple assays (chromosome morphology, GLD-1 staining, functional tests) converge on the same conclusion.

result: Three stress conditions that reduce germ cell division (starvation, high NaCl, absence of sperm) permit maintenance of germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch in 48-79% of gonadal arms. This suggests cell-cycle quiescence itself is an effector of stem cell maintenance. However, this maintenance is not simply due to M-phase inhibition, as cdk-1 RNAi does not permit GLP-1/Notch-independent maintenance.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 provide evidence from multiple quiescence-inducing conditions with adequate sample sizes (n=129-231). The negative result with cdk-1 RNAi (C70) is important for ruling out a simple model and is confirmed by synaptonemal complex visualization. However, the partial penetrance (48-79%) for high NaCl and sperm absence is lower than for starvation (99%), which could indicate mechanistic differences or technical limitations.

result: Starvation inhibits the meiotic entry of transient progenitors, similar to its effect on germline stem cells.
evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by the emb-30 experiments comparing re-feeding to continued starvation (Figure 4). After 6 hours of re-feeding, proximal progenitor zone cells entered meiosis, while continued starvation showed minimal meiotic entry. The experimental design appropriately restricts cell movement to distinguish transient progenitors.

result: Starvation-induced quiescence is mechanistically distinct from DNA damage-induced G2 arrest. DNA damage causes CDK-1 phosphorylation, nuclear enlargement, and requires cep-1/p53, while starvation-induced quiescence shows none of these features.
evaluation: Claims C72-C79 provide three independent criteria distinguishing starvation-induced quiescence from DNA damage arrest, with direct experimental evidence for each (Figure 7A, 7B). The phospho-specificity of the CDK-1 antibody was validated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). This is important for understanding the mechanism of quiescence.

result: Starvation-induced quiescence in adult germ cells does not individually require genes in the TGF-β, insulin/IGF-1, or AMPK pathways, nor factors affecting neuropeptide processing, secretion, or chemosensation. Exogenous serotonin does not affect quiescence. This suggests adult quiescence is controlled differently than larval responses and is largely independent of behavioral responses to food.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 provide a comprehensive genetic screen with adequate sample sizes (n=46-452 gonadal arms). The negative results are important for ruling out known nutrient-sensing pathways. However, the conclusion is limited to stating these genes are not individually required, leaving open the possibility of redundancy or involvement of untested pathways.

result: Historical and current understanding of stem cell quiescence: Adult stem cells were once thought to be universally quiescent, but it is now clear they cycle according to tissue needs. Some stem cells switch between quiescence and proliferation in response to stimuli, and perturbations affecting the cell cycle can impact stemness.
evaluation: Claims C1, C89-C94 provide appropriate context from the literature with proper citations. These are background claims establishing the scientific context and motivation for the study. They accurately represent the field's understanding.

result: The C. elegans adult germline is a tractable model system with simple linear organization. The progenitor zone contains distal germline stem cells and proximal transient progenitors that cycle continuously under fed conditions. Prior to this work, germ cell proliferation in adults had not been examined in detail under food-limited conditions.
evaluation: Claims C10-C15, C95-C96 provide appropriate characterization of the model system with proper citations to prior work. These establish the foundation for the current study and accurately represent established knowledge about C. elegans germline organization.

result: Prior work in other systems: In Drosophila, nutrient limitation affects germ cell proliferation and stem cell number. In C. elegans, primordial germ cells arrest in G2 until larvae feed, and starvation from L4 causes reversible germline shrinkage through programmed cell death and oogenesis.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 accurately summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings and establish what was known before this study.

result: Facultative stem cell quiescence contributes to germline shrinkage during starvation because dividing cells are not replaced, and contributes to re-growth by enabling rapid cell-cycle re-entry upon re-feeding.
evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are reasonable inferences connecting the current findings to prior observations of germline shrinkage. The logic is sound: if cells stop dividing (current finding) and cells are lost to death/oogenesis (prior work), then the tissue will shrink. The rapid re-entry observation directly supports C102.

result: The G2-to-M transition is emerging as a primary point of cell-cycle control in C. elegans germ cells and may be a conserved feature of eukaryotic cell-cycle control. C. elegans germ cells arrest in G2 during multiple developmental stages, G2 length is highly variable even under fed conditions, and G1 is very short. Similar G2 control is observed in yeast, Tetrahymena, Drosophila, and mammals.
evaluation: Claims C103-C120 synthesize current findings with extensive prior work across multiple organisms. The current data (C108, C109) combined with prior work (C105-C107, C112-C119) support the inference that G2-to-M control may be conserved (C120). The argument is well-constructed with appropriate citations.

result: This work establishes the C. elegans germline as a model of facultative stem cell quiescence and demonstrates its utility in clarifying the role of quiescence in maintaining the stem cell state.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are appropriate summary statements of the study's contributions. The work does establish C. elegans as a model for facultative quiescence (supported by all the experimental data) and demonstrates utility by showing quiescence can maintain stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch (C6-C9, C63-C69).

result: Summary of main findings: Adult germ cells in C. elegans become quiescent in the absence of food, characterized by slowed S phase and G2 arrest. This quiescence maintains germline stem cells independent of GLP-1/Notch signaling. Re-feeding causes rapid exit from quiescence and resumption of GLP-1/Notch requirement.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 accurately summarize the major findings of the study, which are well-supported by the experimental data discussed in other result groups. These are appropriate summary statements for the Discussion section.

result: Cell-cycle quiescence in C. elegans germ cells is characterized by slowing of S phase, block to M-phase entry, and rapid re-entry capability. This quiescence alters genetic requirements for stem cell maintenance: GLP-1/Notch signaling, required under fed conditions, becomes dispensable during quiescence, demonstrating that quiescence itself can maintain stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C3-C9 represent the core findings of the manuscript. C3-C5 are supported by the cell-cycle analysis data (Figures 2-3). C6-C9 are supported by the glp-1(q224ts) temperature-shift experiments (Figure 6). These claims are well-integrated and represent the major conceptual advance of the paper.
